# Evidence: chronological evaluation (auto-generated by evaluate.py)

Labelled, de-duplicated claims: 11146 (141 fraud). Post-1-May-2026 (the regime the test set is in): 1422 claims, 36 fraud.

**Protocol.** Walk-forward over June 2026, retrained every 7 days. Outcomes are assumed to be known 30 days after a claim, so a model retrained on date s trains only on claims submitted up to s-30 days, and partner fraud-history features (for training and validation claims alike) use only labels from claims up to min(claim date - 30 days, training cutoff). A brute-force audit re-derives these features for sampled rows in every fold and checks that no label newer than the cutoff is read.

## 1. Main result: June 2026 walk-forward (final model type = logistic regression, post-May rows weighted 10x)
n=713, fraud=22, AUC=0.642, AP=0.165 (base rate 0.031), top-40: 9 fraud caught (precision 22%, recall 41%), Rs 13,132 stopped, 31 genuine held, net Rs 1,352
95% bootstrap CI over claims: AUC 0.48-0.81, AP 0.08-0.34, net Rs -7,493 to Rs 12,849.
Alternative cost view: also charging the Rs 260 contact cost per reviewed claim -> net Rs -9,048.
Leakage audit: PASSED (5 folds, 1400 rows re-derived by brute force).

By week (the model has more post-change training data later in the month): 2026-06-01: n=147, fraud=6, AUC=0.17; 2026-06-08: n=191, fraud=5, AUC=0.95; 2026-06-15: n=158, fraud=4, AUC=0.80; 2026-06-22: n=164, fraud=7, AUC=0.82; 2026-06-29: n=53, fraud=0, AUC=nan

## 2. Cold-start check: May 2026 (no post-change training data exists yet)
n=709, fraud=14, AUC=0.357, AP=0.015 (base rate 0.020), top-40: 0 fraud caught (precision 0%, recall 0%), Rs 0 stopped, 40 genuine held, net Rs -15,200
Interpretation: right after the 1-May policy change a model trained only on the old regime cannot find the new fraud; it needs weeks of post-change labels. With a 30-day label lag that wait is real, and it is the main reason June is weaker than a naive backtest suggests.

## 3. Sensitivity (June walk-forward; every row obeys the same leakage rules with its own lag)
| variant | AUC | AP | caught@40 | net Rs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| logistic, w=10, lag 30d (FINAL TYPE) | 0.642 | 0.165 | 9 | 1,352 |
| logistic, w=1 (no up-weighting) | 0.514 | 0.041 | 2 | -11,271 |
| logistic, w=20 | 0.651 | 0.209 | 10 | 3,280 |
| boosted trees, w=10 | 0.615 | 0.071 | 3 | -10,114 |
| boosted trees, w=20 | 0.615 | 0.080 | 2 | -12,796 |
| logistic, w=10, lag 14d (if outcomes were known faster) | 0.864 | 0.403 | 15 | 11,691 |
| logistic, w=10, lag 0d (outcomes known instantly - unrealistic upper bound) | 0.888 | 0.463 | 16 | 13,566 |
| hand rule (small+uninspected+new partner), same lag-30 history | 0.896 | 0.491 | 16 | 13,552 |
| hand rule without any history features | 0.908 | 0.334 | 14 | 7,912 |

The model type stays logistic regression: boosted trees are not clearly better here, and logistic is simpler to explain. The hand rule needs no training and is competitive, which is a finding in itself. Weights and model type were chosen after earlier looks at June, so even these corrected numbers are somewhat optimistic.

## 4. Does a higher score mean higher fraud risk? (June walk-forward, score deciles)
| decile (10 = highest score) | claims | fraud | fraud rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 72 | 6 | 8.3% |
| 2 | 71 | 0 | 0.0% |
| 3 | 71 | 0 | 0.0% |
| 4 | 71 | 1 | 1.4% |
| 5 | 72 | 0 | 0.0% |
| 6 | 71 | 1 | 1.4% |
| 7 | 71 | 1 | 1.4% |
| 8 | 71 | 0 | 0.0% |
| 9 | 71 | 2 | 2.8% |
| 10 | 72 | 11 | 15.3% |

Spearman correlation between score and outcome: 0.085 (positive = higher score, more fraud). Reading: the top decile holds 11 of 22 frauds (15% vs 3% overall); below it the ordering is mostly noise because fraud cases are so few. Use the score to pick the top ~40-70 claims, not to rank the whole book.

## 5. Error analysis (June walk-forward, top-40 cut-off)
Missed frauds: 13 of 22. Their profile: new partner (<1 yr) 11, small uninspected 12, claimed Rs 1,900-1,999 1, median amount Rs 1,164, partner had no confirmed fraud in (lagged) history 10, median score rank 458 of 713.
False alarms in top 40: 31. Profile: new partner 10, small uninspected 25, partner with prior confirmed fraud 16. Most false alarms are genuine small uninspected claims; genuine customers at flagged outlets will sometimes be held (Rs 380 goodwill each).

## 6. Limitations
- Only 22 fraud cases in the June holdout and 36 since the policy change: every number above has wide error bars (see the interval).
- The 30-day label lag is an assumption (the export has no decision dates). Results depend on it strongly (section 3). If investigations close faster, results are better.
- Because of that lag, the June backtest trains on far less post-change data than the final model will have, so it is conservative on that point. The final model is trained on all labelled claims through 30 Jun 2026 and its test scores cannot be validated here (outcomes hidden).
- Model type and weights were chosen after earlier looks at June. No untouched labelled holdout exists, so treat section 1 as an upper-leaning estimate.
- Scores are not calibrated probabilities (post-May rows are up-weighted). Use them for ranking only.
- Partner history only covers partners already seen. A brand-new bad outlet is caught only through the small-uninspected, amount and customer signals.
- Legacy Zoho 'not fraud' labels may include undecided cases exported as 0 (cannot be identified), so older negatives are slightly unreliable.
- Re-submitted claim_ids: the first submission is kept. Free text, serials and timestamps were not used (no signal found / unreliable).
- Fraud may adapt once the model is used (outlets can move amounts below Rs 1,900). Retrain monthly and track real outcomes of the flagged claims.
